study_identification_part.si4_title: Delineating the Heterogeneity of Alzheimer's Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment Using Normative Models of Dynamic Brain Functional Networks

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To elucidate the heterogeneity of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) by constructing sex-specific normative age models of dynamic brain functional networks, mapping individual deviations, and identifying robust neurophysiological subtypes based on deviation patterns from resting-state fMRI data.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score deviation for each dynamic functional network feature; calculated as (observed - predicted) / sqrt(prediction_uncertainty^2 + variance); site-adjusted z-scores (mean NC deviation per site used as baseline)
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The methods section provides the exact formula for calculating deviation z-scores. The z-score quantifies how much each individual differs from the healthy pattern in each dynamic functional network. The paper also describes that to avoid site influence, they computed the mean deviation of NC participants as a baseline for each site and adjusted the z-scores accordingly. Each patient's deviation pattern was represented by 34 z-scores (17 networks × 2 features).
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: Using the normative model, each feature of each participant from dataset 2 and dataset 3 of the same age was positioned on the normative trajectory percentile. A deviation z score for quantifying a given brain functional network's feature was created from the normative range as follows: [formula] where ŷ denotes the predicted value of the feature, y represents the observed value, σ₁ is the prediction uncertainty, and σ₂ is the variance obtained from the normal distribution (34). The z score estimates how much each individual differs from the healthy pattern in each dynamic functional network. To avoid the influence of multiple sites on the calculation of deviations, we computed the mean deviation of the NC participants as a baseline for each site and adjusted the z scores for patients with MCI and AD accordingly. Finally, each patient's dynamic functional pattern was presented by 34 deviation z scores as a deviation pattern

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: K-means clustering (100 repetitions) on 34-dimensional deviation patterns to identify subtypes; optimal cluster number determined using 28 indices from NbClust package; validation with BIRCH clustering algorithm; Spearman correlations to assess deviation pattern similarity between subtypes; two-sample t-tests with age, sex, and head motion as covariates for group comparisons of deviation patterns, functional connections, and structural features (FDR correction at α=0.05); ANOVA and post-hoc t-tests for cognitive measures (MMSE, MoCA) with age and sex as covariates; Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank test for MCI-to-AD progression risk; linear regression models with age and sex as covariates to estimate cognitive decline trajectories over time; replication experiments using Power-264 and Schaefer-200 atlases with confusion matrices to quantify robustness
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Two distinct subtypes of AD and MCI were identified based on dynamic functional connectivity deviation patterns: subtypes with positive deviations (AD-1, MCI-1; ~40-44% of patients) showing increased connectivity and GMV, and subtypes with negative deviations (AD-2, MCI-2; ~56-61% of patients) showing decreased connectivity and GMV, with MCI-2 demonstrating higher AD conversion risk and faster cognitive decline.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study identified two consistent subtypes each for AD and MCI based on deviation patterns from normative models of dynamic functional connectivity. In Dataset 2, 43.6% of MCI patients were classified as MCI-1 (n=112) and 56.4% as MCI-2 (n=145); 39.3% of AD patients were classified as AD-1 (n=116) and 60.7% as AD-2 (n=179). AD-1 and MCI-1 subtypes exhibited predominantly positive deviation patterns in a-FCS and f-FCS, particularly in sensorimotor network (SM), ventral attention network (VAN), default mode network (DMN), and limbic system (LIM), with increased functional connectivity strength and gray matter volume in DMN-related regions (potentially compensatory). In contrast, AD-2 and MCI-2 showed significant negative deviation patterns across all brain regions, especially in SM, dorsal attention network (DAN), and DMN, with decreased functional connectivity and reduced gray matter volume/cortical thickness in precuneus, cingulate gyrus, and anterior cingulate lobe. The deviation patterns showed high positive correlations between corresponding subtypes (r=0.89, p<0.0001 for AD-1 vs MCI-1 and AD-2 vs MCI-2), suggesting MCI subtypes may transform into corresponding AD subtypes. In Dataset 3 longitudinal analysis, MCI-2 showed higher AD conversion risk (p=0.028) and more rapid cognitive decline in everyday language abilities, memory, and visuospatial abilities compared to MCI-1. AD-1 had higher MMSE scores than AD-2 (p=0.005). The 10-fold cross-validation of normative models showed high robustness (SMSE=0.960±0.038, MSLL=-0.018±0.021). Results were validated using alternative clustering algorithms (BIRCH with >80% consistency) and different atlases (Power-264, Schaefer-200).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Multi-site scanning protocol variability; lack of longitudinal data in the in-house dataset (Dataset 2); relatively small sample size for MCI longitudinal analysis; uncertainty about correspondence between subtypes derived from different imaging modalities/features
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Several limitations of the current study should be considered. First, scanning protocols varied across datasets and sites. To mitigate site effects on the calculation of deviations, we computed the mean deviation of the NC participants as a baseline for each site to adjust the deviations for patients accordingly. Second, longitudinal data were unavailable in the in-house dataset, so we used the participants with MCI from ADNI as an independent site for validation. We also noted that the sample size of the MCI group with longitudinal data is relatively small, which cautions us to interpret some of the results carefully. Finally, various neuropathological patterns identified across different imaging modalities may give rise to distinct subtypes. The extent to which the subtyping findings derived from other features/modalities correspond to overlapping patient subgroups remains unclear, presenting a challenging area of research

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Site-specific baseline adjustment for deviations: computed mean NC deviation per site and adjusted patient z-scores accordingly to minimize multi-site effects; 100-repeated clustering procedure to ensure stability of subtype identification (average stability >95%); confusion matrices used to validate clustering robustness across different algorithms and atlases; subtypes replicated across two independent datasets (MCAD and ADNI) demonstrating genuine biological differences

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study used dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) features rather than static FC, which provides a novel perspective on brain functional heterogeneity. The study trained 34 separate normative models (17 networks × 2 features: a-FCS and f-FCS) using sex-specific Gaussian process regression. Dataset 2 (MCAD) was a multi-center dataset with 7 different sites using different 3T scanners (Siemens Trio Tim, Siemens Skyra, GE Signa HDx, Siemens Verio). The study adjusted for site effects in deviation calculation but not during normative model training (which used single-site data). The dynamic FC features were calculated using a sliding time window of 60 seconds. The Yeo-17 network template was used to decompose FC matrices into 17 functional networks. Clustering stability for subtype identification was very high (>95% average across 100 repetitions). The study provides evidence that heterogeneity in AD may begin to manifest during the MCI stage, suggesting MCI and AD represent a continuum of similar heterogeneity patterns.
